# Single line-to-ground faults

A single line-to-ground (LG) fault connects one phase conductor to ground through a fault impedance. In symmetrical components the positive-, negative- and zero-sequence networks are connected in series at the fault point, so the fault current has all three sequence components. At the fault the voltage of the faulted phase falls toward zero when the fault resistance is low, while the voltages of the other two phases change much less. In this project the LG fault types are AG, BG and CG.

A line-to-line (LL) fault connects two phase conductors without a ground connection. Only the positive- and negative-sequence networks take part, connected in parallel at the fault point, and no zero-sequence current flows. The voltages of the two faulted phases move toward each other. In this project the LL fault types are AB, BC and CA.

# Fault resistance and detectability

Fault resistance limits the fault current and reduces the voltage depression that remote sensors see. A high-resistance fault therefore leaves a weaker signature. This project simulates three fault resistances: 0.1, 1 and 10 Ω. The 10 Ω faults are the hardest to localize: for the standard RGSAGE-Max model the macro-F1 is 0.949 at 0.1 Ω, 0.893 at 1 Ω and 0.676 at 10 Ω (RESULTS.md section 1).

# What a μPMU measures

A micro-phasor measurement unit (μPMU) measures voltage and current phasors at distribution level with precise time stamps from a common time reference, at a high reporting rate. IEEE Std C37.118.1 defines the synchrophasor measurement requirements. In this project each of the 25 μPMUs provides three RMS phase voltages per time step to the model, together with three availability-mask channels.

# Measurement noise is not sensor dropout

Noise leaves the availability mask at 1, so the pattern that dropout-aware training learns to recognise never appears. Dropout-aware training therefore does not help against measurement noise. For the standard model at no dropout the macro-F1 falls from 0.846 to 0.786, 0.579 and 0.345 as the noise standard deviation grows from 0.0005 to 0.002 and 0.01 per unit. Noise and dropout together can push the result below the always-no-fault baseline of 0.0256.

A wrong value from a present μPMU (a silent failure) also leaves the mask at 1. The GridSense gate has no silent-failure check (ablation step A3 is not run), so a report cannot exclude a wrong reading from a present μPMU.

# Ambiguity sets

An ambiguity set is a group of candidate fault locations that produce nearly the same measurements at the available sensors, so the data cannot separate them. Which candidates are indistinguishable depends on which sensors are available. When the evidence is ambiguous a report should show the candidates and not a single bus. # How a voltage sag spreads along a feeder

During a fault the voltage is lowest at the fault point and recovers with electrical distance from it. The depth of the sag at a sensor depends on the impedance between the sensor and the fault compared with the impedance between the fault and the source. Sensors close to the fault therefore carry the most information about its location. This is why losing the sensors nearest to a fault (targeted dropout) hurts more than losing random sensors.

# The soft vote

The model classifies each of the 25 nodes separately. The decision for a window sums the 25 node softmax vectors and takes the class with the largest sum. The summed vector adds up to 25, not to 1. # Calibration and isotonic regression

A confidence is calibrated when predictions made with confidence p are right about a fraction p of the time. Expected calibration error (ECE) measures the gap; this project uses 15 equal-mass bins. # Dropout-aware training

Dropout-aware training masks random μPMU nodes while the model is trained. For each training batch the number of masked nodes k is drawn from {0, 1, 2, 5}, and the model learns that the mask pattern (0,0,0) means a dark sensor. # Measurement noise is not sensor dropout

Noise leaves the availability mask at 1, so the pattern that dropout-aware training learns to recognise never appears. Dropout-aware training therefore does not help against measurement noise. For the standard model at no dropout the macro-F1 falls from 0.846 to 0.786, 0.579 and 0.345 as the noise standard deviation grows from 0.0005 to 0.002 and 0.01 per unit. Noise and dropout together can push the result below the always-no-fault baseline of 0.0256.

A wrong value from a present μPMU (a silent failure) also leaves the mask at 1. The GridSense gate has no silent-failure check (ablation step A3 is not run), so a report cannot exclude a wrong reading from a present μPMU.

# Line-to-line faults

A line-to-line (LL) fault connects two phase conductors without a ground connection. Only the positive- and negative-sequence networks take part, connected in parallel at the fault point, and no zero-sequence current flows. The voltages of the two faulted phases move toward each other. In this project the LL fault types are AB, BC and CA.

# Single line-to-ground faults

A single line-to-ground (LG) fault connects one phase conductor to ground through a fault impedance. In symmetrical components the positive-, negative- and zero-sequence networks are connected in series at the fault point, so the fault current has all three sequence components. At the fault the voltage of the faulted phase falls toward zero when the fault resistance is low, while the voltages of the other two phases change much less. In this project the LG fault types are AG, BG and CG.
